title: Parrot Seed Diet Calculator 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
description: Calculate exact daily seeds, fruits & veggies for parrots, budgies & cockatiels by species and weight. Free, instant, vet-aligned results.
intro:
Feeding a pet bird sounds simple until you realize that a budgie's nutritional needs are almost nothing like a macaw's—and that getting the balance wrong can silently shorten your bird's life. Obesity, feather-destructive behavior, fatty liver disease, and calcium deficiencies are among the most common preventable health problems in companion parrots, and most of them trace back to a single root cause: an unbalanced, seed-heavy diet given without any real measurement or species awareness.

For decades, the default advice was a bowl of mixed seeds topped off whenever it looked low. Modern avian nutrition research has completely overturned that approach. We now know that seeds—while palatable and energy-dense—are high in fat and low in vitamins A, D3, calcium, and amino acids that psittacine birds need daily. An all-seed diet for a cockatiel is roughly the equivalent of feeding a child nothing but potato chips: they'll eat enthusiastically, but the long-term consequences are serious.

The challenge pet owners face is translating the research into practical daily portions. How many grams of leafy greens does a 90-gram cockatiel actually need? What fraction of a conure's diet should come from fresh fruit before natural sugars become a problem? How do you scale those numbers up when you have a 1,200-gram blue-and-gold macaw? These are the questions this Parrot Seed Diet Calculator is built to answer.

By entering your bird's species and body weight, the calculator applies species-specific ratios derived from established avian nutrition guidelines—combining seed allowances, fresh produce targets, and formulated pellet recommendations into a single, easy-to-read daily feeding plan. The output accounts for the fact that smaller birds have faster metabolisms relative to their body mass, that lories and lorikeets require nectar-based nutrition that is radically different from seed-eating psittacines, and that breeding or molting birds have temporarily elevated protein and fat requirements.

What makes this tool genuinely useful in daily practice is its specificity. Rather than telling you to feed 'a small handful,' it gives you measurable amounts in grams and tablespoons, broken down by food category. You can use those numbers to set up a weekly prep routine—washing, chopping, and portioning fresh food in advance—which is one of the most effective ways to maintain dietary consistency for your bird.

This calculator is not a substitute for an avian veterinarian, but it gives you a defensible, evidence-informed baseline to work from—and a concrete starting point for the conversation when you do visit one.

explanation:
**Bird nutrition** follows international veterinary guidelines from organizations like WSAVA and AAHA. Feeding requirements, preventive care, and behavior enrichment vary significantly by species, age, weight, and individual activity level.

## How It's Calculated

This calculator distributes daily seeds, fruits, and vegetables based on your bird's species and weight. Using international avian nutrition standards, it recommends optimal daily portions for your bird's health and wellbeing.

The calculator applies the formula to your inputs, verifying typical ranges and alerting you when values fall outside safe guidelines for your specific bird species.

## Important Notes

These recommendations are informational only. For critical decisions about your bird's health and nutrition, consult a qualified avian veterinarian or specialist. Data is current through 2026 and regularly updated based on the latest avian nutrition research.

faq.q: How much should I feed my parrot or budgie every day?
faq.a: Daily food amounts depend on your bird's species, body weight, and life stage—not just the size of the bowl. As a general framework validated by avian nutrition research, a bird should consume roughly 10–15% of its body weight in fresh food daily, adjusted for caloric density. A 35-gram budgie needs approximately 1.5 teaspoons of seeds per day alongside fresh produce. A 480-gram African grey needs around 2–3 tablespoons of mixed food. A 1,100-gram macaw may need 4–5 tablespoons of varied food plus foraging enrichment. The key mistake most owners make is offering food ad libitum (freely available at all times) with no measurement—this consistently leads to selective eating, where birds pick out the highest-fat seeds and ignore everything else. Using measured daily portions forces dietary variety and prevents nutritional imbalances. This calculator gives you species-specific gram and tablespoon targets rather than vague 'handful' estimates.

faq.q: What's the ideal ratio of seeds to pellets to fresh food?
faq.a: The ratio that avian veterinarians and nutritionists most commonly recommend for most psittacine species is approximately: 50–60% high-quality formulated pellets as the dietary foundation, 30–40% fresh vegetables and limited fruit, and 10–20% seeds, nuts, and other treats. Seeds are not nutritionally complete—they are high in fat, low in vitamins A and D3, and deficient in calcium and essential amino acids. Pellets, by contrast, are formulated to meet full nutritional requirements. However, many birds raised on seeds resist pellets initially, so transitioning gradually—reducing seeds by 10% per week while introducing pellets—is usually more successful than an abrupt switch. Fresh vegetables are non-negotiable: dark leafy greens, bell peppers, squash, carrots, and cooked legumes provide carotenoids, vitamin C, and fiber that pellets alone cannot replicate. Fruit should be offered sparingly (no more than 10% of diet) due to its high natural sugar content.

faq.q: Do different parrot species really need different diets, or is a standard mix fine?
faq.a: Species differences in diet are significant enough that a 'one mix fits all' approach can cause real harm over time. Lories and lorikeets are nectarivores—their digestive systems are adapted for liquid nectar and pollen, not dry seeds, and feeding them a standard seed mix causes digestive failure. Hyacinth macaws have an unusually high fat requirement and naturally eat palm nuts with very high lipid content; their diet legitimately includes more nuts than most other species. African greys have notably high calcium demands and are prone to hypocalcemia, making leafy greens and calcium-supplemented pellets especially important. Eclectus parrots have a uniquely long digestive tract and are particularly sensitive to artificial colors, flavors, and preservatives in processed pellets—fresh food makes up an unusually high proportion of their healthy diet. Budgies and cockatiels, while closely related in practice as beginner birds, have different tolerances for certain foods: cockatiels handle small amounts of millet better, while budgies are more prone to obesity on high-fat diets.

faq.q: Which foods are toxic and should never be offered to parrots?
faq.a: Several common human foods are dangerous or fatal to parrots and should be kept entirely away from birds. Avocado contains persin, a fungicidal toxin that causes respiratory distress, weakness, and cardiac failure in birds—even small amounts can be lethal. Chocolate and caffeine affect the bird's nervous system and can cause seizures and death. Onions and garlic (raw or cooked) cause hemolytic anemia by destroying red blood cells. Apple seeds, cherry pits, and peach stones contain amygdalin, which metabolizes into cyanide. Alcohol, even trace amounts from fermented fruit, is toxic. High-sodium foods (chips, pretzels, canned foods) damage the kidneys. Mushrooms of many varieties are toxic to birds. Rhubarb leaves contain oxalic acid. Dairy products are not toxic per se but birds lack lactase and cannot digest lactose, leading to digestive upset. When in doubt about a new food, check with an avian veterinarian before offering it.

faq.q: How do I know if my bird is at a healthy weight?
faq.a: The most reliable way to monitor a bird's weight is a digital kitchen scale that reads in grams, used consistently at the same time of day (typically before the first morning feeding). You should record weights weekly and graph them over time—a trend is more informative than any single reading. For physical assessment, gently part the feathers over the keel (breastbone): in a bird at healthy weight, the keel has a slight ridge that you can feel but that does not protrude sharply. If the keel feels sharp like a knife edge, the bird is underweight. If you cannot feel it at all because it's cushioned by fat deposits, the bird is overweight. Species-specific healthy weight ranges vary: budgies typically 30–45 g, cockatiels 75–125 g, African greys 400–600 g, blue-and-gold macaws 900–1,300 g. If your bird is outside those ranges, consult an avian vet before making dietary changes independently.

faq.q: Should I adjust food portions if my bird is molting, breeding, or more active than usual?
faq.a: Yes, and the adjustments are meaningful. Molting is metabolically expensive—growing new feathers requires significant protein and specific amino acids (particularly methionine and lysine). During molt, increase protein-rich foods by roughly 15–20%: cooked egg, cooked legumes (lentils, chickpeas), or a protein-enriched supplement recommended by your avian vet. Breeding hens have dramatically elevated calcium needs to produce eggshells—cuttlebone and mineral blocks should always be available, and leafy greens rich in calcium (kale, bok choy) should be offered daily. Chicks in the nest require crop-milk and soft foods; breeding pairs often need increased caloric intake of 20–30% above maintenance. For activity level: birds with large flight cages or regular out-of-cage flight time burn more calories and may need portions increased by 10–15%. Sedentary cage-bound birds need careful portion control to prevent obesity.

faq.q: How should I introduce fresh vegetables if my bird refuses to eat them?
faq.a: Vegetable refusal is extremely common in birds raised exclusively on seeds, and it requires patience rather than force. The most effective strategy is systematic desensitization combined with social eating cues. First, place vegetables in the food bowl alongside familiar foods for two weeks without removing the seeds—the goal is familiarity, not immediate consumption. Next, try 'eating' the vegetables yourself in front of your bird: parrots are flock animals and are powerfully motivated by watching flock-mates eat. Third, offer vegetables skewered on a kabob or tucked into foraging toys so that interacting with them becomes play. Fourth, try different preparation methods: some birds prefer raw bell pepper but cooked sweet potato; others eat shredded greens but reject whole leaves. Finally, use the 'chop' method: finely dice 8–10 vegetables together so the familiar smell of one masks the unfamiliar smell of others. Consistency over weeks is the key—don't give up after three rejections.

faq.q: Can I prepare my bird's food in advance and store it?
faq.a: Yes, weekly prep is one of the most practical ways to maintain a consistent, varied diet for your bird. Fresh vegetables can be washed, dried thoroughly, chopped, and stored in airtight containers in the refrigerator for 4–5 days safely. Leafy greens hold up well for 3–4 days; softer items like mango or banana are best prepared fresh daily or one day ahead. Many owners use the 'chop' technique: a large batch of 10–15 finely diced vegetables and cooked grains prepared weekly, portioned into daily servings, and frozen in ice-cube trays—then one cube is thawed overnight per bird per day. Cooked legumes (lentils, chickpeas) can be batch-cooked, cooled completely, and refrigerated for 3 days or frozen for a month. Never offer food that has been sitting in the cage for more than 4 hours, especially in warm conditions, as bacterial growth accelerates rapidly in moist bird food.

faq.q: What role do pellets play, and how do I transition a seed-addicted bird?
faq.a: Pellets are the single most important improvement most bird owners can make to their bird's diet. High-quality formulated pellets (brands recommended by avian vets include Harrison's Bird Foods, Zupreem Natural, and Roudybush) are nutritionally complete, meaning they provide balanced vitamins, minerals, amino acids, and trace elements in every bite—unlike seeds, where a bird can selectively eat only its favorite items. The transition from seeds to pellets is the most common challenge avian vets address. The recommended approach is gradual: start by offering pellets in a separate dish alongside seeds. After two weeks, begin reducing seeds by 10–15% per week while maintaining pellet availability. Monitor weight closely throughout—if your bird loses more than 10% of its body weight during transition, slow down the process. Never withhold food to force pellet acceptance, as birds can go into hypoglycemic crisis within hours. A bird that sees you eating a pellet, or watches another bird eat one, will often try it voluntarily.

faq.q: Is water quality and availability important for parrots?
faq.a: Water is critically important and frequently overlooked. Parrots should have access to clean, fresh water at all times. In the wild, many species travel significant distances to reach clean water sources daily. Chlorinated tap water is generally safe for most birds, though some owners use filtered water, particularly for sensitive species like African greys. Water dishes should be cleaned and refilled at least once daily—twice daily in hot weather or if the bird bathes in its water dish (common behavior). Bacteria multiply rapidly in warm water contaminated with food particles. Stainless steel or ceramic dishes are preferable to plastic, which scratches over time and harbors biofilm. Some birds prefer drinking from a drip bottle or water fountain—if your bird uses a bottle, check daily that it is actually dispensing and not vacuum-locked. Dehydration in birds is an emergency; if your bird stops drinking for 24 hours alongside lethargy or fluffed feathers, contact an avian vet immediately.

faq.q: How do I use the calculator results in practice day to day?
faq.a: The calculator gives you daily targets by food category—seeds/nuts, fresh vegetables, fresh fruit, and pellets—expressed in grams or household measurement equivalents. The most practical implementation is a two-bowl system: one bowl with the measured seed and pellet portion for the day, and a second bowl with the day's fresh food. Prepare the fresh bowl each morning and remove it after 4 hours to prevent spoilage, then offer the seed/pellet bowl for the remainder of the day. Weigh your bird weekly and note whether portions need slight adjustment upward or downward based on weight trends. Keep a simple feeding log for the first month—a notes app with date, weight, and any refusals is enough—so you can identify patterns. If your bird consistently leaves large amounts of one food category, it may signal a preference issue, illness, or that portion size needs adjustment. Bring your feeding log and calculator outputs to annual avian vet visits so the vet can assess diet quality alongside physical health metrics.

faq.q: Is this calculator a substitute for an avian veterinarian's advice?
faq.a: No, and it's important to be clear about that. This calculator provides a science-informed baseline for daily feeding amounts based on species and weight—it is a practical starting point, not a clinical prescription. Every bird is an individual: underlying health conditions, medication interactions, reproductive status, feather condition, and behavioral factors all influence nutritional needs in ways that require hands-on veterinary assessment. Annual wellness exams with an avian-certified veterinarian (look for board-certified avian vets or members of the Association of Avian Veterinarians) are the standard of care for companion parrots. At those visits, the vet can assess body condition score, run bloodwork to detect subclinical deficiencies, evaluate feather quality, and give diet recommendations specific to your bird's current health status. Use this calculator to arrive at those appointments informed and with a concrete diet plan to discuss—rather than starting the conversation from zero.
